vignette:
Daniel, a 54-year-old civil servant in a long-term relationship, first began to understand that the worst of his symptoms were tied to a period when he had been physically abused by a former romantic partner, a man who could turn intimidating with little warning and who often cornered him at home. Daniel described the relationship as one in which control had mattered in the smallest details, and the moments that still set off his fear were not abstract reminders but concrete situations that recreated that old helplessness: being left alone in a room or building, sleeping alone or in an unfamiliar place, or finding himself alone with men. He said it was the feeling of not being able to control what happened next that was most frightening. When he was left alone in a room or building, or found himself alone with men, that same helpless feeling would bring the whole episode back into his mind in a rush, as if the memory had been waiting just beneath the surface for those moments. In those moments his body seemed to brace before his mind had fully caught up, and over time he came to organize his life around avoiding that state.

At work, in the civil service offices where he spent his days surrounded by colleagues and clients, Daniel noticed that he kept himself constantly in motion and in company. He would linger at desks, volunteer for minor errands, and arrange calls or coffee with coworkers so that he was never left by himself with his thoughts, and never at risk of being alone with men in a quiet corridor or empty meeting room. At home, he resisted sitting in a room by himself for long and would move from one occupied space to another, partly because he felt safer with other people nearby and partly because being alone made the memories crowd in. He had come to believe that staying surrounded by people was the only way to keep the past at a distance, even though the habit left him exhausted and increasingly dependent on the presence of others. The more he tried to push it away by staying busy, staying with people, and never letting himself settle alone with his thoughts, the more the memory seemed to remain intact and ready to break through when he was finally on his own.

The memories themselves were not easy for Daniel to summon deliberately. When a therapist or a trusted friend asked him to describe what had happened, he found it difficult to access the story in any orderly way, as if the details sat just beyond reach. Yet when the memory arrived on its own, it did so with a vividness that startled him. He would see it in photographs in his mind: the layout of the room, the posture of the man, the angle of the furniture, each image sharp and frozen. He also noticed something more bodily and disturbing, as if the event had left a taste that could return unchanged in the present. A sudden flash of that taste would make him feel pulled back into the moment, and that sensory quality made the scene feel not remembered but re-experienced.

Those memory fragments fed directly back into the situations he feared. If he found himself alone in a building after hours, or in an unfamiliar hotel room when work required travel, the photographs in his mind would begin to assemble themselves around him, and his sense of danger would sharpen. Being alone with a man, even a colleague he otherwise liked, could make his thoughts rush toward what had happened before, as though the memory were warning him that the same loss of control might return. Once those images and sensations were active, Daniel’s urge to escape into company or keep moving became stronger, and his need to avoid solitary places or one-to-one male encounters hardened into routine.

That routine, however, also seemed to keep the memories alive. Because he rarely let himself sit with what had happened, he remained unable to make much sense of the sequence of events, and when the memory surfaced it did so in the same startling, pictorial way, with the same strange taste attached to it. The more he detached himself from the recollection, the more foreign and fragmentary it felt, and the more easily it could burst back in when he was alone. Daniel recognized a painful irony in this: the strategies that helped him get through the day also made the memory return in its most vivid form, and every return of the memory made the ordinary facts of solitude and male presence feel newly dangerous. Over months, this pattern narrowed his life; he accepted fewer invitations, avoided staying overnight in unfamiliar places, and arranged his schedule so he would not have to be by himself.

By the time he sought help, Daniel was increasingly aware that he was living around fear rather than through his days. He came in because the effort of constant socialising and avoiding solitude was wearing thin, and because his relationship had begun to feel strained by how often he needed reassurance and company. What frightened him most was not only the memory itself, but the possibility that he would keep organizing his life around it forever. What he hoped for was to be able to sit alone in a room, travel for work, and be around other men without feeling that old loss of control close in on him.

violations.explanation: The vignette shows triggers leading to avoidance, but it does not clearly state that triggers directly bring on the memory within the same paragraph.
The vignette says avoidance keeps the memories alive, but it does not explicitly convey that maladaptive strategies drive or lead to the memory itself in a causal way within the same paragraph.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Memory: The vignette shows triggers leading to avoidance, but it does not clearly state that triggers directly bring on the memory within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "The smell of his cologne in the lift sent the whole night flooding back before she had even reached her floor."
  e.g. "Hearing that song on the radio dragged her straight back into the room where it happened, as if no time had passed at all."
  e.g. "Walking past the bus stop where it occurred, she was no longer on the street — she was back there, every detail sharp and close."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: The vignette says avoidance keeps the memories alive, but it does not explicitly convey that maladaptive strategies drive or lead to the memory itself in a causal way within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
